In Leeds, the maths test came back with a red 9 out of 30 and a line at the bottom: Parent signature, please. Jamal stared at it through lunch. At home he copied his mum's name from a birthday card and signed it at the kitchen table, pressing too hard.
On Wednesday his teacher said she would phone home about extra help. Jamal told her the phone was broken. On Thursday he told his friend Liam he'd got 25. Each lie needed another, and each sat heavier in his stomach. He kept checking his mum's phone for missed calls.
On Friday night, when she asked why he wasn't eating, Jamal pushed the test across the table and burst into tears. She read it slowly, then reached for his hand.

qa.q: What score was written on Jamal's maths test?
qa.a: A red 9 out of 30 was written on the maths test.

qa.q: How did Jamal feel as the lies grew during the week?
qa.a: He felt more and more afraid; each lie sat heavier in his stomach and he kept checking his mum's phone for missed calls.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could have ended it sooner?
qa.a: Signing the test himself forced more lies; showing it to his mum on the first day would have been hard but would have ended the fear much sooner.

qa.q: How might Jamal's mum feel when she reads the test?
qa.a: She may feel sad that Jamal was so scared to tell her, and reaching for his hand suggests she wants to comfort him more than scold him.

grounding: A boy hides a low mark by signing for his mother, and each cover-up needs another lie until the fear becomes too heavy to carry.

The Class 6 unit-test sheets were handed out in the school library, and Payal's science paper said 11/40. She folded it into her atlas.
The next day the circular came: parent-teacher meeting on Saturday. Payal told Ma'am that her mother was travelling. At home she said there was no meeting. When Rashmi asked at recess, "Is your mummy coming Saturday?", Payal said, "She's out of town," and felt her face burn, because her mother was right at home making dinner.
By Friday she couldn't sleep. What if Rashmi's mother phoned hers? What if Ma'am checked? Every new lie felt like another brick in a wall she had to keep holding up.
On Saturday morning she walked into the staffroom alone, holding the folded paper.

qa.q: Where did Payal hide her science paper?
qa.a: Payal folded it into her atlas.

qa.q: What was Payal worried about on Friday night?
qa.a: She worried that Rashmi's mother might phone hers or that Ma'am would check, and that all her lies would come out.

qa.q: How could Ma'am support Payal when she walks into the staffroom?
qa.a: Ma'am could thank her for coming, stay calm about the mark, and talk with Payal and her mother together about extra help.

qa.q: What might Rashmi think if she later learns Payal's mother was at home?
qa.a: Rashmi might feel confused or a little hurt at being lied to, though she may also understand that Payal was scared.

grounding: A schoolgirl hides a low mark and a parent meeting, and every cover-up adds to the fear it was meant to end.

Saurabh Sir flipped through the signed maths tests and stopped at Lavanya's. The 9 out of 25 at the top was circled in red, and the signature underneath was in blue gel pen, the same pen Lavanya wrote with.
"Lavanya, your mother signed this?"
"Yes, Sir." The word came out before she could stop it.
"Good. Then please ask her to meet me on Friday about the next test."
Lavanya's stomach dropped. Now Mummy had to come on Friday, and Mummy didn't know anything. At lunch she couldn't eat. She could say Mummy was sick on Friday, but then she'd need another excuse, and another.
In the last period, she walked slowly to Saurabh Sir's desk, holding the test. "Sir," she whispered, "she didn't sign it. I was scared."

qa.a: The 9 out of 25 at the top was circled in red.

qa.q: Why couldn't Lavanya eat at lunch?
qa.a: She felt trapped and afraid, because one lie about the signature now needed more lies to hide it from Mummy on Friday.

qa.q: How could Saurabh Sir support Lavanya now that she has told the truth?
qa.a: He could thank her for coming to him, stay calm, and help her tell her mother about the mark together.

qa.q: How might Saurabh Sir feel when Lavanya comes to his desk?
qa.a: He might feel concerned and relieved, noticing how scared she was and glad she chose to tell him.

grounding: It shows a schoolchild forging a signature out of shame and finding that each cover-up demands another lie and grows the fear.

Wednesday. Nandini got her English test back: 11 out of 30. She folded it into a tiny square and pushed it to the bottom of her bag. At home, when Amma asked about the test, she said, "Not given back yet."
Friday. Her friend Kavitha said loudly on the school van, "Nandini, what did you get? I got 22." Nandini said, "I forgot to look." Kavitha frowned. Nandini's hands were cold. Now Kavitha might tell her mother, who might tell Amma.
The next Tuesday was parent-teacher day. Nandini lay awake the night before, heart pounding. In the morning, she took it out, smoothed it on the table, and said, "Amma, I lied. I got eleven." Amma looked at the paper, then at her face, and sat down beside her.

qa.q: What mark did Nandini get on her English test?
qa.a: She got 11 out of 30.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel on the night before parent-teacher day?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid, lying awake with her heart pounding because the hidden test and the lies were about to come out.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what finally helped?
qa.a: Each lie needed another one and made her fear grow; showing Amma the test herself ended the cover-up.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha when Nandini says she forgot to look?
qa.a: Kavitha finds it strange and is a little puzzled, because a test result is not something people usually forget.

grounding: It shows a child hiding a low mark and needing more lies over several days, with the fear growing each time until she tells the truth.

Siddharth, beta, you're hiding that report card like it's a snake. Come, let your Hafsa Nani tell you something.
When I was your size, I got a red mark in arithmetic. I was so ashamed that I tore the page out of my report book and hid it in the flour tin. Then my teacher asked why the page was missing, and I said my little brother tore it. Every day there was a new story to remember, and I shook whenever the flour tin was opened.
One morning my mother found the page, white with flour. She didn't shout. She only said, "You carried this alone for three weeks?" I cried from relief. The red mark was not half as heavy as the lies.

qa.q: Where did young Hafsa hide the torn page?
qa.a: She hid it in the flour tin.

qa.q: How did young Hafsa feel while the page was hidden?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and constantly frightened, shaking every time the flour tin was opened because of all the stories she had to keep straight.

qa.q: What turning point in the story ended her fear?
qa.a: When her mother found the page and asked gently instead of shouting, Hafsa could stop lying and finally felt relief.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's little brother have felt when she blamed him?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and unfairly accused, since he was pulled into a lie he knew nothing about.

grounding: A grandmother tells how a child's shame led to hiding a bad mark, and how each cover-up needed another lie until the truth brought relief.

Madhav's maths test said 9 out of 25 in red ink, and it had to come back signed by tomorrow. Mummy was on night shift at the hospital and wouldn't be home till morning.
He sat at the table under the flickering tube light, heart thumping. He practised her signature on scrap paper eleven times. The twelfth looked almost right. He signed.
The next day Ms Rao looked at it a second too long. "Your mother usually signs in blue," she said. "This is black."
"She... used my pen," Madhav said. Then he had to ask his sister Binita to say Mummy had borrowed his pen, in case Ms Rao called.
By evening he had three lies to remember and a stomach ache. Binita looked at him across the dinner table. "Just tell Mummy," she whispered. "It's getting too big."

qa.q: What did Madhav's maths test say?
qa.a: 9 out of 25 in red ink.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel by evening?
qa.a: Madhav felt anxious and weighed down, with three lies to remember and a stomach ache.

qa.q: What would help Madhav most now?
qa.a: Telling Mummy the truth when she is home, as Binita suggested, before more lies are needed to hold up the first one.

qa.q: How might Binita feel being asked to help cover the lie?
qa.a: Binita seems worried and uncomfortable, which is why she whispers that it's getting too big.

grounding: Shows a child forging a signature on a low mark out of shame, and each cover-up needing another lie that grows the fear.
